## 10. Willingness to Pay

### 10.1 Fixed Coefficients

When the price variable has a *fixed* coefficient $\alpha = \beta_p$ (a column of $X$), the WTP for any fixed attribute $k$ is the usual marginal rate of substitution, with the same analytic delta-method SE as in the MNL case (§8 of the MNL document):

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k = -\frac{\beta_k}{\alpha},
\qquad
\nabla g = \begin{pmatrix} -1/\alpha \\ \beta_k/\alpha^2 \end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{SE}} = \sqrt{\nabla g^T \hat{V}_{(k,p)} \nabla g}
$$

### 10.2 Random Coefficients

For a random attribute coefficient $\beta_k(\eta)$ the WTP is itself a random variable $-\beta_k(\eta)/\alpha$, and a scalar summary must be chosen. The summaries reported follow the package's parameterization (§1.3):

**Normal RC with estimated mean** (`rc_mean = TRUE`, `rc_dist[k] = 0`): $\beta_k = \mu_k + (L\eta)_k$ has mean $\mu_k$, so the **mean WTP** is

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k = -\frac{\mu_k}{\alpha}
$$

with the linear-ratio gradient of §10.1 applied to $(\mu_k, \alpha)$.

**Shifted log-normal RC with estimated location** (`rc_mean = TRUE`, `rc_dist[k] = 1`): $\beta_k = \exp(\mu_k) + \exp((L\eta)_k)$. Since $\beta_k$ is monotone in the normal draw $(L\eta)_k$ and the median of $\exp((L\eta)_k)$ is $\exp(0) = 1$, the population **median** is $\exp(\mu_k) + 1$ and the **median WTP** is

$$
\mathrm{WTP}_k^{\text{med}} = -\frac{\exp(\mu_k) + 1}{\alpha},
\qquad
\frac{\partial g}{\partial \mu_k} = -\frac{\exp(\mu_k)}{\alpha},
\qquad
\frac{\partial g}{\partial \alpha} = \frac{\exp(\mu_k) + 1}{\alpha^2}
$$

The median is preferred to the mean, $\exp(\mu_k) + \exp(\sigma_k^2/2)$ with $\sigma_k^2 = (LL^T)_{kk}$, because the mean is highly sensitive to the estimated variance (a thin right tail dominates it).

**Shifted log-normal RC without location** (`rc_mean = FALSE`, `rc_dist[k] = 1`): $\beta_k = \exp((L\eta)_k)$ has median exactly 1, so the median WTP is $-1/\alpha$ with $\partial g / \partial \alpha = 1/\alpha^2$ — uncertainty comes solely from $\hat\alpha$.

**Normal RC without mean** (`rc_mean = FALSE`, `rc_dist[k] = 0`): the mean is 0 by construction; no WTP row is reported.

### 10.3 Random Price Coefficients Are Rejected

The implementation requires `price_var` to be a fixed-coefficient column of $X$ and
rejects every random price coefficient. For a normally distributed denominator this is
substantively important: positive density arbitrarily close to zero generally makes
$E|\beta_k/\alpha|$ diverge. That no-moment argument does **not** cover every possible
mixing distribution—for example, inverse moments of a sign-constrained log-normal can be
finite—but `wtp()` still does not simulate the joint ratio distribution, account for its
correlation, or report its quantiles. Thus the rejection is both a specification guard
for normal price mixing and an implementation boundary for other distributions. WTP-space
estimation (Train and Weeks 2005) is not implemented in `choicer` v0.2.0.

*Code reference: [R/wtp.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/wtp.R)*

---

## 11. Consumer Surplus and the Simulated Logsum

### 11.1 Expected Logsum

Conditional on a coefficient realization $\beta(\eta)$, expected maximum utility over
the iid type-I extreme-value errors is
$\log \sum_j \exp(V_{ij}(\eta))+\gamma_E$, where $\gamma_E$ is Euler's constant. As in
the other package methods, `logsum()` omits this scenario-invariant additive constant.
The mixed-logit logsum integrates over the mixing distribution:

$$
\mathrm{logsum}_i = \mathbb{E}_\eta\left[\log \sum_{j \in C_i} \exp\big(V_{ij}(\eta)\big)\right]
\;\approx\;
\frac{1}{S} \sum_{s=1}^{S} \log \sum_{j \in C_i} \exp\big(V_{ij}^s\big)
$$

simulated over the same deterministic Halton draws used in estimation (regenerated from the stored draw metadata), with the outside option contributing $\exp(0)$ in each draw's sum when present, and the max-subtraction trick applied per draw.

**Order of operations matters.** The log-sum-exp function is convex, so by Jensen's inequality

$$
\frac{1}{S}\sum_s \mathrm{lse}(V^s) \;\geq\; \mathrm{lse}\left(\frac{1}{S}\sum_s V^s\right),
$$

with strict inequality when the draws induce non-common variation in utilities. A
nondegenerate $\Sigma$ alone is not sufficient for strictness: if the random contribution
is the same additive shift for every available alternative, log-sum-exp is affine in that
direction and equality holds. A dedicated C++ kernel (`mxl_logsum`) computes the per-draw
logsum and then averages across draws.

### 11.2 Expected Consumer Surplus

With a *fixed* price coefficient $\alpha$ (the marginal utility of income $-\alpha$ is then nonrandom):

$$
\mathbb{E}[CS_i] = \frac{\mathrm{logsum}_i}{-\alpha}
$$

A random price coefficient is rejected for the capability and specification reasons in
§10.3; the divergence argument applies directly to normal price mixing but not to every
sign-constrained distribution. As in MNL, the formula assumes no income effects. The
routine does not enforce $\alpha<0$; the economic interpretation as positive marginal
utility of income requires the analyst to verify that sign. CS levels inherit the ASC
normalization, so only differences across counterfactual scenarios are meaningful. The
implementation reports point estimates for MXL (the delta-method SE of mean CS is
currently provided for MNL only); Krinsky--Robb resampling is a practical interval method.

*Code reference: [R/surplus.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/surplus.R); kernel in [src/mxlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mxlogit.cpp) (`mxl_logsum`)*

---

## 12. Goodness of Fit

The measures are model-agnostic and identical to §10 of the MNL document, computed from the simulated log-likelihood and simulated choice probabilities:

- **McFadden pseudo R²**: $R^2 = 1 - \ell(\hat\theta)/\ell_0$, adjusted $R^2_{\text{adj}} = 1 - (\ell(\hat\theta) - K)/\ell_0$, with $K$ counting all estimated parameters ($\beta$, $\mu$, Cholesky block, ASCs).
- **Equal-shares null** (default; exact for unbalanced choice sets and weights): $\ell_0 = -\sum_i w_i \log(M_i + \mathbf{1}_{\text{outside}})$.
- **Market-shares null** (constants-only closed form):
  $\ell_0 = c\sum_j N_j \log(s_j)$, where $c$ is the common weight, valid only
  for identical choice-set composition and uniform weights. The constants-only model
  contains no random coefficients, so the MNL closed form applies unchanged.
- **Hit rate**: weighted share of choice situations whose observed choice has the highest *simulated* probability $\bar{P}_{ij} = \frac{1}{S}\sum_s P_{ij}^s$; with an outside option, the kernel returns the simulated outside probability directly and the outside good competes for the maximum.

*Code reference: [R/gof.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/gof.R)*

---

## 13. Conditional (Individual-Level) Tastes

`conditional_tastes()` recovers, for each likelihood unit, the mean and standard deviation
of the random coefficients *conditional on the choices observed* — the same posterior draw
weights $\omega_{ns}$ that build the panel score and Hessian (§2.6, §3.5, §4.5), now applied
to the realized taste draws themselves rather than to the score:

$$
E[\beta_n \mid y_n, x_n; \hat\theta] \approx \sum_{s=1}^S \omega_{ns}\, \beta_{ns},
\qquad
\mathrm{SD}(\beta_n \mid y_n, x_n; \hat\theta) \approx
  \sqrt{\sum_{s=1}^S \omega_{ns}\,(\beta_{ns} - \bar\beta_n)^2},
$$

with $\beta_{ns} = \mu^*_\cdot + \gamma_{ns}^{*}$ the taste at draw $s$ on the scale it
enters utility (§1.1–1.3), $\bar\beta_n$ the conditional mean above, and $y_n$ the sequence
of choices observed across $n$'s $T_n$ situations (Revelt and Train 2000; Train 2009,
ch. 11). $T_n \equiv 1$ defines the same object for the default cross-sectional fit, one
choice situation at a time; a single choice reveals comparatively little, so its conditional
mean sits closer to the population mean than a panel decision maker's typically does.

**Not $\beta_n$ itself.** $E[\beta_n \mid y_n, x_n; \hat\theta]$ is the average taste among
decision makers who would make $n$'s choices, not $n$'s own realized $\beta_n$ — it shrinks
toward the population mean, more so the fewer situations $n$ contributes. Consequently the
*variance across* decision makers of the conditional means understates $\Sigma$: by the law
of total variance,
$$
\mathrm{Var}(\beta) = \underbrace{\mathrm{Var}_n\bigl(E[\beta_n \mid y_n]\bigr)}_{\texttt{revealed}}
  \;+\; \underbrace{E_n\bigl[\mathrm{Var}(\beta_n \mid y_n)\bigr]}_{\texttt{residual}},
$$
so the `revealed` share ($w_n$-weighted variance of the conditional means) and the
`residual` share ($w_n$-weighted average of the conditional variances) should sum to about
one. These are numerical checks, not specification tests: for normal random coefficients
with free means, both this identity and $\texttt{mean\_cond} \approx \texttt{model\_mean}$
are the likelihood's first-order conditions for $\mu$ and $\Sigma$ — the population mean
and variance are exactly the $\omega$-weighted mean and variance the estimating equations
set to zero at $\hat\theta$ — so they hold at a converged maximum whatever the true taste
distribution. A departure points to too few draws $S$ or an unconverged $\hat\theta$; when
a coefficient's mean is fixed at zero (`rc_mean = FALSE` and no fixed coefficient on the
same variable), a `mean_cond` far from zero can also flag that restriction. For log-normal
coefficients the variance identity holds on the underlying normal scale $\gamma$, not the
utility scale $\beta$ reported here, so expect departures of a few percent in either
direction at moderate $S$. `print.choicer_tastes()` reports these alongside
`model_mean`/`model_sd` (the moments of $f(\beta \mid \hat\theta)$ itself, §1.2–1.3) and
`mean_cond`/`sd_cond` (the weighted mean and SD of the conditional means across units).

**Implementation.** `mxl_conditional_tastes_parallel()` reuses `mxl_unit_load()` and
`mxl_unit_simulate()` (§3.5) to obtain $\omega_{ns}$ per unit, then forms
$\bar\gamma_n = \Gamma_n\,\omega_n$ over the unit's $K_w \times S$ realized-deviation block
$\Gamma_n$ (the same $\gamma_{ns}^{*}$ values already used to build $V_{ij}^s$, §1.1) and
adds back the mean block, $\bar\beta_n = \mu^* + \bar\gamma_n$; the SD uses the analogous
weighted second moment of $\Gamma_n$ around $\bar\gamma_n$. Both are matrix-vector products
— no second pass is needed, since neither quantity is an outer product. Units whose
log-likelihood is non-finite — possible only when their utilities overflow (§4.5, §5.4) —
return `NA` and are dropped from the population summary.

*Code reference: `mxl_conditional_tastes_parallel()` in
[src/mxlogit.cpp](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/src/mxlogit.cpp);
[R/conditional_tastes.R](https://github.com/fpcordeiro/choicer/blob/main/R/conditional_tastes.R).*
